Q: How can I install the Composer dependency manager when its installer has issues with my php.ini file? A:

I had no idea there was a windows installer for composer.
I'm glad the ini approach worked but there are a lot of other packages out there which could be useful to your project. Eventually, you'll need composer.

May I suggest an alternative approach?
You'll need to use the command line.
Powershell or cmd should do the trick.

You can do everything with composer without actually 'installing' anything. To use composer, download the phar file form the composer download page , e.g. latest stable composer.phar, and put it in your project folder.

Open your cmd prompt and navigate to your project folder.
php.exe composer.phar init

This will init composer and create a composer.json file for you to manage the project dependencies.

Then you can use the same terminal to add phpdotenv or any other library to your project. (There are a ton of them on packagist.org.)

php.exe composer.phar require vlucas/phpdotenv
and it will download the library, place it in a "vendor" folder for you.

You'll need to modify your app to make use of it.
Composer includes an autoloader so you don't have to manually load all the libraries its managing for you.

Add require __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';
to the top of your project and composer will autoload libraries as you declare them.

Q: Why can't you pass props from +layout.svelte to +page.svelte files in SvelteKit? A:

The limitation might exist because the framework has its own properties that need to be set. This way there is no confusion over where the properties come from and it prevents future property name conflicts in case a new property has to be added.

Note that data from layout load functions is merged across the hierachy, so if you need to pass anything from a +layout to a +page, you can use this as a mechanism.

Q: Looking for deeper understanding of std::launder and compiler behavior A:

Cross-file optimization is a thing in practice (e.g. GCC or Clang -flto for link-time optimization, or gcc -fwhole-program *.cpp). The ISO C++ standard doesn't put any restrictions on optimizations across compilation-units or make things not UB based on that.

But yeah in practice you can hide things from the optimizer if they're in separate libraries or you don't use LTO within one executable or library. But that would mean an actual inefficient call in the asm, vs. just telling the compiler how to treat this object.

And it doesn't let the compiler know the old object's lifetime has ended, like if you want to reuse space from an int* for a float*, the strict-aliasing rule allows the compiler to assume that an int* and float* point to different memory. In your case you're only just returning a float* to your std::byte storage used to hold a different float, so the compiler does have to assume this float* could point to the float it already knows about (whose lifetime hasn't ended as far as it knows.)

Q: How can I use specific values for query in Apache IoTDB A:

You can do it in one query (if your IoTDB version supports subqueries):

SELECT time, s1, s2, s3, s4
FROM root.sg.d1
WHERE s1 = (SELECT MAX(s1) FROM root.sg.d1);

This returns all rows where s1 is at its maximum, including s2, s3, and s4.

If your version doesn’t support subqueries, you’ll need to run two queries (first get MAX(s1), then filter by that value).

Q: Fixing plotting artifacts when using plt.xscale('symlog') A:

You can simple change plt.xscale('symlog') to plt.xscale('log'). 'symlog' is an extension of the 'log' scale for negative values, which you do not need here. Naturally, this extension is not seamless, and it needs to remove values under a small threshhold. That is what is causing you issues here.

Be careful if you need to plot for values starting at 0.1, you need to change t at the begining.

Full code:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

t = np.logspace(-1, 4, 100)

CP = 400
P_an = 1100
tau = 30

P = CP+P_an/(1+t/tau)

dP_dPan = 1/(1+t/tau)
dP_dtau = (P_an*t)/(tau**2*(1+t/tau)**2)


S_CP = CP/P
norm_pan = (dP_dPan - dP_dPan.min()) / (dP_dPan.max() - dP_dPan.min())
norm_tau = (dP_dtau - dP_dtau.min()) / (dP_dtau.max() - dP_dtau.min())


plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))
plt.plot(t, norm_pan, label=r'$\text{P}_\text{an}$')
plt.plot(t, norm_tau, label=r'$\tau$')
plt.plot(t, S_CP, label="CP")

plt.vlines(tau, 0, max(norm_tau), linestyles=':', colors="dimgray", alpha=.4, lw=1.5)

plt.xscale('log')
plt.xlim(0.1, 10001)
plt.ylim(0, 1.05)

ax = plt.gca()
ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)

ax.set_xticks([1, 10, tau, 100, 1000, 10000])
ax.set_xticklabels([1, 10, r'$\tau$', 100, 1000, 10000])

plt.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc='center right')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
